To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) serum ALT is not a reliable biomarker of acetaminophentoxicity; 2) serum AST, GGT, ALP and LDH are not reliable biomarkers of acetaminophentoicity; 3) serum ALT, AST, GGT and LDH are reliable biomarkers of hepatocellular injury; 4) serum ALP is not a reliable marker of hepatobiliary injury; and 5) serum ALT and AST are reliable biomarkers for predicting

(1) the biomarkers AST and ALT are not specific to acetaminophen hepatotoxicity, (2) ALT is a more specific biomarker than AST, (3) AST and ALT are poor predictors of evolving liver injury, and (4) ALT is a better predictor of mortality in acetaminophentoxicity than AST.

1) serum ALT and AST levels are not reliable indicators of the severity of acetaminophenen-induced acute liver injury, and 2) serum biomarkers that reflect the severity of liver injury, such as ALT/AST, are not reliable predictors of the risk of acute liver failure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel biomarkers to facilitate the diagnosis of acetaminophem-induced acute liver injury, and to predict its severity.
the development of novel biomarkers for acetaminophene-induced acute liver injury, and the identification of mechanisms underlying the toxicity of acetaminophene.

the development of a biomarker panel for acetaminophem-induced acute liver injury that can be utilized to confirm the diagnosis of acute liver injury, predict severity, and/or guide therapeutic interventions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current state of the art in acetaminophenspecific biomarker development has not reached a point that would be useful in the clinic.
the development of biomarkers for acetaminophem toxicity remains an area of active research and that no single biomarker has yet to be identified.
there is still a long way to go to validate a biomarker for the clinical diagnosis of acute liver injury.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are no validated biomarkers for acetaminophem-induced acute liver injury.
there is a need for further research to develop a validated panel of biomarkers to improve diagnosis and management of acetaminophene-induced acute liver injury.
the development of new biomarkers for the diagnosis and/or prognosis of acetaminophene-induced liver injury is an important area of study and will be an important area of research in the future.
The main takeaway from our work is that
biomarker development is an iterative process that requires careful evaluation of candidate biomarkers and the development of new biomarker panels.
the combination of biomarkers, which are mechanistically linked to different phases of the injury, may be more useful than any single biomarker.

the combination of a biomarker panel, including alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransfrase, bilirubin and a biomarker of oxidative stress such as malondialdehyde or 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine, is likely the best approach for diagnosis.
